content.title: Grid: Two Dimensions
content.hook: Flexbox is excellent when the main relationship is one direction.
content.context:
Grid is useful when you care about rows and columns together.

A dashboard of repeated cards often has that shape: the cards form a shared structure across both dimensions.
goals: Understand when Grid is useful for a two-dimensional arrangement and create a simple row-and-column layout.

content.title: Create a grid

options.text: Create three columns that share the available space.

feedback.correct: `fr` represents a fraction of the available grid space. Three equal `1fr` tracks create three equal flexible columns here.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. In `grid-template-columns`, each `1fr` track claims one equal share of the available width, so `1fr 1fr 1fr` defines three flexible columns.

content.title: Flex or Grid?
content.text:
You have three related controls that should sit in one horizontal group.

Flexbox is a natural fit.

You have a dashboard that needs a shared row-and-column structure.

Grid is a natural fit.

The point is not that one tool is “better.” The point is that the relationship tells you which tool is easier to reason about.

activities.title: Tiny lab
activities.instruction: Update the `.dashboard` grid rule so the six cards arrange into three equal columns with a 16px gap, then run the preview.

content.prompt:
Right now `.dashboard` arranges the six cards into 2 columns (`1fr 1fr`) with an `8px` gap.

Update `.dashboard` so it uses three equal flexible columns (`grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr;`) and `gap: 16px;`, then run the preview to see the six cards form two rows of three.
content.htmlFixture:
Card 1Row 1
Card 2Row 1
Card 3Row 1
Card 4Row 2
Card 5Row 2
Card 6Row 2

feedback.correct: Your CSS includes `display: grid;`, `grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr;`, and `gap: 16px;`. In the preview, the six cards now share three equal column tracks across two rows.
feedback.incorrect: Check your `.dashboard` rule: keep `display: grid;`, set `grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr;` for three equal columns, and set `gap: 16px;`.

content.question:
Change the template to:

```css
grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr;
```

What should you expect?

options.text: The grid now has two flexible columns.
The grid becomes a single image.

feedback.correct: The number of column tracks changed from three to two. The rows then form around that two-column structure.
feedback.incorrect: Look closely at `grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr;`: two `1fr` values define two flexible column tracks, so the six cards reflow into three rows of two.

content.question: Which statement is the strongest beginner rule?

options.text: Use Grid when the layout relationship is naturally described by rows and columns.
Always use Grid for every layout.
Never use Grid for repeated cards.
Use Grid only when changing text color.

feedback.correct: The useful choice is relationship-first. Grid is strong when rows and columns are part of the structure you need.
feedback.incorrect: Avoid all-or-nothing rules. Choose Grid when the layout relationship requires shared row-and-column structure across two dimensions.

activities.title: Replicate UI: Two-Column Metric Grid
activities.instruction: Convert the stacked metric cards into a 2×2 CSS Grid with two equal columns and a 12px gap.

content.prompt: Apply `display: grid`, `grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr`, and `gap: 12px` to `.metric-grid` so the four cards form a balanced two-column grid.
hints: Set `display: grid;` on `.metric-grid` so the parent controls both rows and columns.
Define two equal-width tracks with `grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr;` and `gap: 12px;`.

styleRules.description: Sets a 12px gap between grid tracks on .metric-grid

feedback.correct: Your `.metric-grid` container now uses `display: grid` with two equal tracks and a 12px gap to arrange the four cards in two dimensions.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite yet — `.metric-grid` still needs `display: grid;`, `grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr;`, and `gap: 12px;`.

content.title: Forge takeaway & Lesson completion
takeaways: **Mental model:** Flexbox is a strong tool for one main direction; Grid is a strong tool for two-dimensional row-and-column relationships.
**Senior habit:** Choose the tool from the relationship, not from a favorite snippet.
**Mastery signal:** You can explain why a repeated card area is naturally expressed as a grid instead of merely memorizing `display: grid`.
